title: Adding Across and Looking Away
author: Text Savvy
summary: An anonymous math-education writer publishing as Text Savvy closes out a serialized series on teaching fractions by tackling addition and subtraction. The core pedagogical claim is that the persistent "adding across" misconception (treating 1/2 + 1/2 as 2/4) is not a student error to be drilled away but a symptom of a poorly constructed instructional narrative about what fractions are. The author's fix is to anchor the whole unit around denominator-as-unit-of-measure, so that converting to common denominators before adding follows naturally from the same conceptual thread used throughout the series rather than arriving as an arbitrary new rule. Before getting to the math, the piece includes a lengthy polemic against professional niceness in education circles, arguing that reflexive politeness lets bad pedagogical ideas and tech-solutionism go unchallenged. The result is part curriculum design and part manifesto for blunt professional criticism.
points: Reframes the decades-old "add fractions across" misconception as a failure of instructional narrative, not student carelessness, arguing fifty years of reform attempts missed the underlying story problem.

Uses denominator-as-unit-of-measure as the throughline concept that makes converting to a common denominator before adding feel like a continuation of earlier lessons rather than a new arbitrary rule.

Argues that professional 'niceness' in education discourse functions as cover for bad ideas and tech-solutionism to spread unchallenged, since critics avoid honest evaluative comment to sidestep discomfort.
Positions the fractions unit as a finished 'story' rather than a checklist of disconnected topics, explicitly rejecting busywork goalposts added merely to satisfy administrative review.
quotes: Even before formal psychological work existed, teacher diaries from the nineteenth century were full of complaints that students would add fractions across, meaning, in this case, a + a = a.
So I looked for a different story for fractions, one that would hammer at this misconception in particular, and found a mathematically and pedagogically coherent narrative to explore.

Unlike other implementations, the denominator as unit of measure concept in my story is not a once-used metaphor; it is what connects intuition with the mathematics, and then weaves them together throughout.
When we add fractions in the same unit, which means that they have the same denominators, we add the numerators and keep the same denominator.
We don't need to invent goalposts for students to fill out the time or look good for a committee review or supervisor.
